questions.question: Design a parking lot system. Walk me through your approach.
questions.interviewer_intent: Classic LLD question — tests OOP design, entity identification, and class relationships
questions.direct_answer: Key classes: ParkingLot (manages floors), ParkingFloor (manages spots), ParkingSpot (tracks occupancy), Vehicle (abstract, with Car/Motorcycle/Truck subclasses), ParkingTicket (tracks entry), FeeCalculator (pricing). Apply Strategy for pricing, Singleton for ParkingLot.

items: ParkingLot: Singleton, holds List<ParkingFloor>, find spot, issue/process ticket
ParkingFloor: holds Map<String, ParkingSpot>, methods for available spots by type
ParkingSpot: spot ID, type enum, occupied flag, park/vacate methods
Vehicle: abstract class with licensePlate, VehicleType; Car/Motorcycle/Truck subclasses
ParkingTicket: generated on entry, tracks vehicle, spot, entry time
FeeCalculator: Strategy pattern for different pricing (hourly, flat)
DisplayBoard: Observer pattern to show availability

answer_sections.content: For a parking lot design, I start by identifying entities. The physical objects: ParkingLot, ParkingFloor, ParkingSpot. The actors: Vehicle (abstract) with Car, Motorcycle, Truck subclasses. The transactional objects: ParkingTicket issued on entry, Payment on exit. The services: FeeCalculator. ParkingLot is a Singleton since there's one. ParkingFloor has a map of spots keyed by spot ID for O(1) lookup. ParkingSpot tracks its occupancy and has a canPark() method that checks if the vehicle type fits. On entry: find available spot → park vehicle → issue ticket. On exit: calculate fee → process payment → free spot → mark ticket paid. FeeCalculator uses the Strategy pattern so I can swap in different pricing without changing ParkingLot.

follow_up_questions: How would you handle multiple parking lot locations?
How would you add support for electric vehicle charging spots?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: Design a parking lot — it's the most common LLD question in the industry, and it tests almost every OOP concept at once.

beats.text: A parking lot design covers entities, relationships, state management, and design patterns all in one go. That's why it's a perennial favorite.

groups.heading: Core hierarchy
groups.text: ParkingLot (Singleton) holds a list of ParkingFloor objects. Each ParkingFloor holds a map of ParkingSpot objects keyed by spot ID for fast lookup.

groups.heading: Vehicles
groups.text: Vehicle is abstract with licensePlate and a VehicleType enum. Car, Motorcycle, and Truck extend it. ParkingSpot has a canPark() method that checks if the vehicle type fits the spot type.

groups.heading: Transactions
groups.text: ParkingTicket is issued on entry — it tracks vehicle, spot, and entry time. On exit, FeeCalculator computes the fee using the Strategy pattern.

groups.heading: Observability
groups.text: DisplayBoard uses the Observer pattern: when a spot's occupancy changes, it notifies the board to update availability counts.

beats.text: candidates miss: narrating the entry and exit flow. Say it explicitly — entry: find spot, park vehicle, issue ticket. Exit: calculate fee, process payment, free spot, mark ticket paid. That shows you've modeled the behavior, not just the structure.

speakable_v2.cap: Parking lot hits Singleton, Strategy, Observer, Factory, and composition all at once. Nail this design and you're ready for 80% of LLD interview problems.
followup_handoff: How would you handle multiple parking lot locations?
How would you add EV charging spots?

questions.question: How does the fee calculation work in your parking lot design?
questions.interviewer_intent: Drill into a specific design decision — tests Strategy pattern application
questions.direct_answer: Use the Strategy pattern: FeeCalculator interface with calculateFee(ParkingTicket). Concrete implementations: HourlyFeeCalculator, FlatRateFeeCalculator, VehicleTypeFeeCalculator. ParkingLot holds a reference to the current strategy.

answer_sections.content: For fee calculation, I use the Strategy pattern. I define a FeeCalculator interface with a single calculate() method that takes a ParkingTicket (which has entry time, vehicle type, spot type). HourlyFeeCalculator multiplies hours parked by the hourly rate for that vehicle type. FlatRateFeeCalculator returns a flat fee. WeekendPricingCalculator might apply different rates on weekends. ParkingLot holds a FeeCalculator reference — at runtime, you can swap the strategy without changing ParkingLot code. This aligns with OCP: adding a new pricing model means adding a new class, not modifying existing ones. BigDecimal for money — never float or double for currency calculations.

follow_up_questions: Why do you use BigDecimal instead of double for fee calculations?
How would you handle free parking for the first 30 minutes?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: Fee calculation is where the Strategy pattern earns its keep — pricing rules change constantly, and you don't want to rewrite ParkingLot every time.

beats.text: Fee calculation uses the Strategy pattern: define a FeeCalculator interface with a single calculate() method, then provide different implementations for different pricing rules.

items: FeeCalculator interface: calculate(ParkingTicket) returns BigDecimal
HourlyFeeCalculator: multiplies hours parked by hourly rate per VehicleType
FlatRateFeeCalculator: returns a fixed fee regardless of time
WeekendPricingCalculator: applies different rates on weekends
ParkingLot holds a FeeCalculator reference — swap it at runtime without touching ParkingLot

beats.text: The ticket carries entry time, vehicle type, and spot type. HourlyFeeCalculator computes the duration, looks up the rate for that vehicle type, and multiplies. Adding a new pricing model means adding a new class — ParkingLot doesn't change.
production trap: never use float or double for money calculations. Always use BigDecimal. Floating-point arithmetic introduces rounding errors that compound in financial systems.

speakable_v2.cap: Strategy pattern for fees: one interface, multiple implementations, swappable at runtime. BigDecimal for the math — always.

questions.question: How would you extend the parking lot design for multiple locations?
questions.interviewer_intent: Test extensibility thinking — can you evolve the design without breaking what exists?
questions.direct_answer: Introduce ParkingLotNetwork (or ParkingManagementSystem) that holds multiple ParkingLot instances. Each ParkingLot remains a complete unit. The network layer handles routing: 'find nearest available spot across all lots.'

answer_sections.content: If there are multiple locations, I introduce a ParkingLotNetwork class. Each ParkingLot is still a complete, independent unit. ParkingLotNetwork holds a List<ParkingLot> and has methods like findNearestLotWithAvailability(Location, VehicleType). This doesn't require changing the existing ParkingLot class at all — OCP in action. For cross-lot operations, ParkingLotNetwork can aggregate availability across all lots or route vehicles to the best option based on proximity. I'd also extract an IParkingLot interface that both ParkingLot and ParkingLotNetwork implement — then calling code works with either one. This follows the Composite design pattern — individual lots and the network both implement the same interface.

follow_up_questions: What design pattern are you applying when ParkingLotNetwork and ParkingLot share an interface?
How would you implement a 'find nearest lot' algorithm?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: Extending a design to multiple locations is a classic follow-up — and it's a perfect test of the Open/Closed Principle.

beats.text: When the parking lot needs to support multiple locations, you introduce a ParkingLotNetwork class. Each individual ParkingLot stays unchanged — that's OCP in action.

items: ParkingLotNetwork holds a list of ParkingLot instances
Add findNearestLotWithAvailability(location, vehicleType) at the network level
Extract an IParkingLot interface so calling code works with either a single lot or the network
This follows the Composite pattern: single lot and network both implement the same interface

beats.text: Calling code asks IParkingLot for an available spot. It doesn't know if it's talking to a single ParkingLot or a ParkingLotNetwork — both implement the interface. The network delegates to whichever individual lot has availability.
non-obvious: don't modify the original ParkingLot class to add multi-location support. Adding ParkingLotNetwork above it is the clean extension — it leaves the existing design untouched.

speakable_v2.cap: Multiple locations = add ParkingLotNetwork above existing ParkingLot. Extract a shared interface. The original class doesn't change — that's OCP at work.
followup_handoff: What pattern are you applying when ParkingLotNetwork and ParkingLot share an interface?

questions.question: What design patterns did you apply in the parking lot design and why?
questions.interviewer_intent: Check ability to articulate pattern choices — shows depth of design thinking
questions.direct_answer: Singleton (one ParkingLot), Strategy (pluggable fee calculation), Observer (DisplayBoard updates when spot status changes), Factory Method (create different vehicle types), Builder (complex ParkingTicket construction).

answer_sections.content: I applied several patterns deliberately. Singleton for ParkingLot — there's one, and having multiple instances would be a bug. Strategy for FeeCalculator — pricing rules change without requiring changes to ParkingLot. Observer for the DisplayBoard — when a ParkingSpot's occupancy changes, it notifies the DisplayBoard to update availability counts; this decouples spot management from display. Factory Method for Vehicle creation — VehicleFactory.create(VehicleType.CAR) returns the right subclass without the caller knowing the exact type. Builder for ParkingTicket — it has many optional fields (entryTime, vehicle, spot, status) and Builder makes construction readable. Each pattern was applied to solve a specific design problem, not just to use patterns.

follow_up_questions: What would the design look like without using the Strategy pattern for fees?
Is the Observer pattern appropriate for real-time display updates at scale?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: Naming the patterns you used — and saying why — is what separates a senior-level answer from a junior one.

beats.text: Design patterns in LLD aren't decoration. Each one solves a specific problem. Be ready to name each pattern and explain the problem it solves — not just that you used it.

groups.heading: Singleton — ParkingLot
groups.text: There's one parking lot. Multiple instances would mean inconsistent state — two instances might both think the same spot is available.

groups.heading: Strategy — FeeCalculator
groups.text: Pricing rules change without requiring changes to ParkingLot. Adding WeekendPricing means a new class, not a modified one.

groups.heading: Observer — DisplayBoard
groups.text: When a spot's occupancy changes, the display needs to update. Observer decouples the spot from the display — the spot doesn't need to know about the board.

groups.heading: Factory Method — Vehicle creation
groups.text: VehicleFactory.create(VehicleType.CAR) returns the right subclass. The caller doesn't depend on the concrete type.

groups.heading: Builder — ParkingTicket
groups.text: Tickets have many optional fields. Builder makes construction readable and safe — no multi-argument constructors.

beats.text: sharp edge: interviewers will ask 'why did you use Strategy here?' Be ready to say: 'because pricing rules change, and I want to add new pricing without modifying ParkingLot — that's OCP.' Pattern name plus reason equals a strong answer.

speakable_v2.cap: Each pattern solves one problem. Know the problem first, then name the pattern — not the other way around.
followup_handoff: What would the design look like without Strategy for fees?
Is Observer appropriate for real-time updates at scale?

questions.question: How would you handle concurrent access to parking spots in your design?
questions.interviewer_intent: Test awareness of thread safety in LLD — important for production Java systems
questions.direct_answer: Use synchronized methods or ConcurrentHashMap for spot lookup. The critical section is the check-and-occupy of a spot (race condition: two cars could both see a spot as available). Use synchronized or ReentrantLock on the spot assignment operation.

answer_sections.content: Concurrency is a real concern in a parking lot system — multiple entry barriers could assign the same spot simultaneously. The race condition is the classic check-then-act: both threads see occupied=false, both park, both think they succeeded. The fix: make the check-and-set atomic. I'd make tryPark() synchronized on the ParkingSpot, or better, use AtomicBoolean for the occupied flag and compareAndSet() for lock-free thread safety. The ParkingFloor's spot lookup also needs to be thread-safe — use ConcurrentHashMap instead of HashMap. For the interview, acknowledging this issue and describing the solution demonstrates production thinking, even if we're designing at the class level.

follow_up_questions: What is a race condition and why does it happen in this parking lot scenario?
When would you use ReentrantLock instead of synchronized?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: Concurrent access to parking spots is a sneaky problem — two cars at different gates can race to claim the same spot.

beats.text: The race condition here is classic check-then-act: two threads both read occupied=false, both proceed to park, both think they succeeded. The fix is to make the check-and-set atomic.

items: Mark tryPark() as synchronized on the ParkingSpot — only one thread can enter at a time
Or use AtomicBoolean for the occupied flag and compareAndSet() for lock-free atomicity
Use ConcurrentHashMap for spot storage in ParkingFloor — avoid HashMap in concurrent context
Return a boolean from tryPark() so callers know if they succeeded

beats.text: AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false, true) atomically checks the current value and sets it — if two threads race, only one gets true back. The other gets false and must find a different spot.

production trap: don't synchronize at the ParkingLot level — that serializes all spot assignments across all floors, which kills throughput. Synchronize at the individual ParkingSpot level so different spots can be assigned concurrently.

speakable_v2.cap: Atomic check-and-set per spot, ConcurrentHashMap for the collection. Mention this proactively — it signals production awareness without being asked.
followup_handoff: What is a race condition and why does it happen here?
When would you use ReentrantLock instead of synchronized?
